1301.event_title: Martin Luther teases Katharina about her worrying
1301.event: In early 1546 Martin Luther was away from home at Eisleben, the town of his birth, while his wife Katharina von Bora stayed in Wittenberg and worried about him. On 10 February he wrote to her with mock solemnity, addressing her as an anxious lady and doctor, and joked that ever since she had started worrying, a fire had nearly broken out at their inn and that her holy worries might make the very earth swallow him up. He told her to pray and leave the worrying to God. Luther died at Eisleben eight days later, on 18 February 1546.
1301.explanation: Luther’s teasing turned his wife’s anxious fussing into a shared joke, a playful exchange that only works between two people secure in each other’s love.
1301.tie_back: The kural advises a small, gentle show of displeasure so that the loved one’s longing can be seen for a moment; Luther’s playful mock-complaint about Katharina’s worrying is the same kind of light, loving game.
1301._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it is a documented example of playful, affectionate pique between spouses, but the kural’s specific scene, a confidante urging the wife to hold back her embrace briefly, has no close historical parallel.

1302.event_title: Chopin and George Sand’s rift is never mended
1302.event: The composer Frédéric Chopin and the novelist George Sand were together for nearly a decade, spending their summers at her country house at Nohant. A family dispute arising from the marriage of Sand’s daughter, Solange, strained their relationship, and in 1847 it ended bitterly. By 1848 the rift was complete, and, as Britannica puts it, pride prevented either of them from making the reconciliation both actually wanted; Chopin, already in poor health, died in 1849.
1302.explanation: A quarrel that might have passed was allowed to harden until it could no longer be undone, ending one of the best-known partnerships of the Romantic era.
1302.tie_back: The kural says a lovers’ sulk is like salt, good in the right measure but ruinous when it runs on too long, and Chopin and Sand let their quarrel run on until it spoiled everything.
1302._accuracy_note: Strong: a quarrel kept up too long through pride until reconciliation became impossible is almost exactly the kural’s warning, though the quarrel concerned family matters rather than a lovers’ pique.

1303.event_title: Gandhi nearly turns Kasturba out of the house, then shuts the gate
1303.event: In early 1898, at the Gandhis’ home in Durban, a Christian Indian guest of so-called untouchable parentage left his chamber pot to be emptied, and Gandhi expected Kasturba to help clean it. She carried it out but was in tears and angry, and Gandhi, furious that she did not do it cheerfully, took her by the hand and dragged her to the gate meaning to push her out. Weeping, she asked whether he had no sense of shame and where she could possibly go; ashamed, he shut the gate, and he later wrote that their many quarrels always ended in peace.
1303.explanation: Gandhi later presented the incident as one of the most shameful of his life, a moment when he added to his wife’s distress instead of easing it.
1303.tie_back: The kural says that refusing to embrace and reconcile a hurt and sulking partner is like heaping fresh pain on someone already suffering, which is what Gandhi came to see he had done before he shut the gate.
1303._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong: a distressed spouse made to suffer more, followed by a turn toward reconciliation, fits the kural, though this was a serious quarrel rather than a lovers’ sulk.

1304.event_title: Charles Dickens separates from his wife Catherine
1304.event: Charles Dickens married Catherine Hogarth in 1836, and they had nine children who survived infancy. After years of growing unhappiness he separated from her in May 1858, and from then on she lived apart from him. A painful public scandal followed, during which, according to Britannica, Dickens did not act with tact, patience or consideration; he even printed a public statement about the separation in his magazine Household Words on 12 June 1858, while Catherine kept a dignified silence.
1304.explanation: Instead of seeking to soothe a wife who was already hurt, Dickens cut her off completely and publicly.
1304.tie_back: The kural says that failing to soothe and win back the one who is hurt is like cutting at the root a creeper that is already wilting, and Dickens’s handling of the separation cut the marriage off at its root.
1304._accuracy_note: Reasonable: neglecting and then cutting off an already wounded spouse matches the kural’s image, though the cause was a deep breakdown of the marriage, not a passing sulk.

1305.event_title: Clementine Churchill warns Winston about his manner
1305.event: In June 1940, with France defeated and a German invasion feared, Clementine Churchill wrote to her husband, Prime Minister Winston Churchill, that a devoted member of his staff had told her he risked being disliked by colleagues and subordinates because of his rough, sarcastic and overbearing manner. She told him she had noticed the change herself and that he was not as kind as he used to be. She urged him to combine his great power with courtesy, kindness and calm; it is the only known letter between them from 1940.
1305.explanation: Clementine’s loving rebuke, written at the height of national crisis, came from someone who cared enough about her husband to tell him what no one else dared.
1305.tie_back: The kural says that the true ornament of good men is the loving pique of their wives, and Clementine’s reproachful letter is a famous case of a wife’s affectionate displeasure helping to make a great man better.
1305._accuracy_note: Strong: a wife’s loving reproach serving as an adornment to a good man is close to the kural, though her letter was serious advice rather than a lovers’ sulk.

1306.event_title: Pablo Neruda publishes The Captain’s Verses anonymously
1306.event: While in exile in Italy, the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda finished writing The Captain’s Verses on the island of Capri in 1952, addressing the poems to Matilde Urrutia. The collection contains poems of love, ecstasy and devotion, but also of fury, including lovers’ anger and quarrels. Later that year he published it anonymously in an edition of fifty copies, fourteen years before he and Matilde legally married.
1306.explanation: Neruda’s book treated anger and quarrelling as part of the full experience of love rather than its opposite.
1306.tie_back: The kural says love without its deeper quarrels and small sulks is like fruit that is over-ripe or still green, and Neruda’s love poems deliberately include fury alongside tenderness.
1306._accuracy_note: Reasonable: a famous love book that gives quarrels their place in love fits the kural’s idea, but it is a literary work, not a documented quarrel between the couple.

1307.event_title: Shen Fu writes Six Records of a Floating Life
1307.event: In 1809 Shen Fu, a man educated as a scholar who earned his living as a civil servant and art dealer, wrote Six Records of a Floating Life, a blend of autobiography and love story. Its first record, The Joys of the Wedding Chamber, describes his marriage to Yun, the artistic girl he had loved since childhood, and their shared pleasures. The third record, The Sorrows of Misfortune, tells of their money troubles and of Yun’s death.
1307.explanation: Shen Fu’s memoir is one of the most famous portraits of married love in Chinese literature, and its happiness is shadowed throughout by how short their time together turned out to be.
1307.tie_back: The kural says that even in lovers’ small quarrels there is a hidden pain, the fear that their time together will not last long enough, and Shen Fu’s record of a loving marriage cut short gives that fear a real-life ending.
1307._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows a loving union that did not last long enough, but the sources do not record the couple fearing this during their quarrels.

1308.event_title: Eleanor Roosevelt discovers the Lucy Mercer letters
1308.event: In 1918 Eleanor Roosevelt discovered that her husband, Franklin D. Roosevelt, was romantically involved with her social secretary, Lucy Mercer. She offered him a divorce, but he refused, for reasons that included his political career and his mother’s financial support, and he agreed to stop seeing Mercer. He later resumed contact with Mercer, who was with him when he died at Warm Springs, Georgia, in 1945.
1308.explanation: Eleanor’s grief produced a promise, but whether her husband truly understood the hurt he had caused is doubtful, since political reasons weighed heavily and the promise was not kept.
1308.tie_back: The kural asks what use grieving is when the beloved does not truly understand that the sorrow is his doing; Eleanor Roosevelt’s experience shows how hollow a reconciliation can be when that understanding is missing.
1308._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it touches the kural’s question of whether a lover recognises the grief he causes, but the case is a betrayal and a political marriage, far from the lovers’ pique the kural describes.

1309.event_title: Abigail Adams tells John to Remember the Ladies
1309.place: Braintree, Massachusetts, and Philadelphia, United States
1309.event: On 31 March 1776, while John Adams was at the Continental Congress in Philadelphia, Abigail Adams wrote to him from Braintree asking that in the new code of laws he would "Remember the Ladies" and be more generous to women than earlier lawmakers, warning playfully that women might start a rebellion of their own. John replied on 14 April that he could not help laughing at her extraordinary code of laws and teasingly called her saucy. Abigail answered on 7 May that she did not think him very generous to the ladies, since men proclaiming liberty for all still insisted on keeping absolute power over their wives.
1309.explanation: The exchange mixes a serious argument for women’s rights with the affectionate teasing of a couple who were completely secure in each other.
1309.tie_back: The kural says that just as water is sweet only in the shade, a sulk is sweet only between those who truly love each other, and the Adamses’ spirited, mock-indignant letters show pique that delights because the love beneath it is never in doubt.
1309._accuracy_note: Reasonable: loving, teasing reproach within a secure marriage fits the kural well, though Abigail’s point was a serious political one and not merely a lovers’ sulk.

1310.event_title: Heinrich Heine's hopeless love for his cousin Amalie
1310.event: As a young man working in Hamburg in the business of his rich uncle Salomon Heine, the German poet Heinrich Heine fell in love with his cousin Amalie, a love that German reference works describe as quiet but hopeless. She did not return it, and when she became engaged to another man in 1821 his old love grew stronger than ever. That disappointed love fed some of the most tender poems in his Buch der Lieder (Book of Songs), published in 1827, which made him widely known.
1310.explanation: Heine's longing outlived a plain refusal and turned into some of the best-known love poetry in German.
1310.tie_back: The kural calls it sheer desire when the heart still wants to be with one who leaves its sorrow unsoothed; Heine's heart kept turning to a cousin who gave it no comfort.
1310._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shows longing that persists for someone who does not respond, but this was an unreturned courtship, not a lovers' quarrel left unsoothed; replaces the Van Gogh/Kee Vos entry, for which no second independent source could be reached.
